slides.title: From vectors to scores
slides.summary: The last layer turns a token's vector into a score for every token in the vocabulary.
body: After the last block, the stream is normalised once more and multiplied by the unembedding matrix (shape [d, V]). That gives one score for every token in the vocabulary. These raw scores are called logits.
Logits can be any number, positive or negative. Higher means "more likely to come next", but they aren't probabilities yet. The next slide turns them into probabilities.

When generating, only the scores for the last token matter, because that's the one predicting what comes next. During training, every position's scores are used, each one predicting the token after it.
The bars on the right are the top 8 logits after "I am learning artificial".

body.note: <mark>This list of 100,000+ scores is everything the model outputs.</mark> Picking a token from it is done by normal code outside the model, and you control how. That's the next two slides.

blocks.html: logits after "I am learning artificial" (top 8 of ~128,000)

figure.alt: After "I am learning artificial", the model outputs raw scores (logits): intelligence 7.6, neural nets 4.6, life 4.2, languages 3.9, sweeteners 3.4. Softmax at temperature 1 turns them into probabilities: 89, 4.4, 3.0, 2.2 and 1.3 percent. Top-p at 0.9 keeps only intelligence and neural nets, rescaled to 95 and 5 percent, and one token is drawn at random: intelligence. For the next step, earlier tokens' keys and values are reused from the KV cache and only the new token's are computed. Everything must fit in the context window: system prompt, chat history, documents and tool results, and the reply so far.
figure.caption: The whole chapter on one page: scores → probabilities → a shortlist → one token, then the cache and the window that make the next step possible. Numbers are illustrative.

slides.title: Softmax and temperature
slides.summary: Softmax turns scores into probabilities, and temperature controls how adventurous the choice is.
body: Softmax, the same function used inside attention, turns scores into probabilities: raise e to the power of each score, then divide by the total, so everything is positive and adds up to 1.
Temperature T is applied first: every score is divided by T, so p = exp(z/T) / Σ exp(z/T). A small T makes the gaps between scores bigger; a large T makes them smaller.

ul: T near 0: the top token gets almost all the probability. The output is predictable and the same each time, but can get repetitive. Good for code and factual answers.
T = 1: exactly the probabilities the model learned.
T above 1: flatter, so unlikely tokens get picked more often. More variety, but more mistakes. Useful in small amounts for brainstorming.

body: Drag the slider and watch "intelligence" go from almost certain to just one option among many.

body.note: This is the temperature setting in every LLM API. Setting it to 0 makes the output almost the same every time, though tiny rounding differences on GPUs can still change it now and then.

code: next_id = probs.argmax()            # greedy, same as T -> 0

slides.title: Picking the next token
slides.summary: Before picking a token at random, the unlikely options are usually cut off, so the model doesn't drift into nonsense.
body: If you pick from all the options, now and then a very unlikely token gets chosen, and one bad token can ruin the rest of the sentence. So most systems cut off the unlikely options first:

ul: Top-k: keep only the k most likely tokens.
Top-p (nucleus sampling): keep the fewest top tokens whose probabilities add up to p. When the model is confident, that's one or two tokens; when it's unsure, many. It adjusts to the situation.
Greedy: always pick the single most likely token. The same as top-k = 1.

body: <mark>The remaining probabilities are rescaled to add up to 1 again, and one token is picked at random, with likelier tokens more likely to be chosen.</mark>
Try top-k = 3, then press Sample a few times. Then try top-k = 1.
code: probs = top_k(probs, k)      # zero all but k largest
probs = top_p(probs, p)      # keep smallest set with sum >= p

slides.title: The KV cache
slides.summary: The keys and values of earlier tokens never change, so they're saved and reused instead of being worked out again every step.
body: Each step runs over the whole text again. But because of the causal mask, earlier tokens never look at later ones, so their keys and values come out exactly the same every step. Working them out again is wasted effort.

The KV cache saves every token's keys and values, in every layer, the first time they're worked out. After that, each step only computes Q, K and V for the one new token, and compares its query against the saved keys and values.

ul: Speed: each step's work drops from O(n²) to O(n). This is what makes long, streamed answers possible.
Memory: the cache grows with every token, in every layer. For long texts it can be bigger than the model itself.
Fixes: GQA (fewer key/value heads), storing the cache with fewer bits, and managing it in fixed-size pages, the way a computer manages RAM (PagedAttention, used by vLLM).

body: Use the sliders to work out the cache size for a typical 8B model, then push the length up to 1M tokens.

body.note: It's memoisation: saving results whose inputs don't change. The trade-off is the classic one: more memory for more speed.

code: q, k, v = proj(x_new)                 # only the new token

slides.title: What the context window really is
slides.summary: The context window is everything the model can see at once. It has no other memory.
body: The context window is the most tokens the model can handle at once. Everything it knows about your chat has to fit inside: the system prompt, the chat history, any documents or tool results, and its own reply so far.

ul: No hidden memory: the model forgets everything between requests. Chat apps send the whole history again every turn. "Memory" features work by saving notes and adding them back into the context.
Longer costs more: more context means more attention work and a bigger KV cache, so long prompts are slower and more expensive.

Prompt caching: if a request starts with exactly the same tokens as a recent one, the provider can reuse the saved KV cache for that opening part. That's why keeping the same system prompt at the start is cheaper and faster.

body.note: The model has no memory of its own; the context is all it has. <mark>If something isn't in the context, the model doesn't know it, no matter how recently you mentioned it.</mark>
A big window doesn't mean the model uses all of it well. Details buried in the middle of a very long context are often remembered less reliably than those near the start or end.
